e-8959.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Rectangular Domains
e-8959.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z = y - 4x$ that is bounded by the constraints $0 \leq x \leq 2$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
e-8959.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z = f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = y - 4x, \qquad 0 \leq x \leq 2, \quad 0 \leq y \leq 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4x)=-4, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4x)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-4)^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+16+1}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{18}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\cdot (2-0)\cdot (1-0) \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9141.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains
e-9141.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the plane $z = 2y+2x$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\cos{x}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
e-9141.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = 2y+2x, \qquad (x,y)\in D,
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq y \leq \cos{x} \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/e74d609a1288446f0f3adc0de65b814f2a6daaf2d398478e7834882f3be68c8c.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y+2x)=2, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y+2x)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =3(1-0) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

e-8948.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as X=F(Y,Z) or Y=F(X,Z)
e-8948.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $x =y+\sqrt 2 z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by the constraints $1 \leq y\leq 2$ and $1 \leq z \leq 3.$
e-8948.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x = y+\sqrt 2 z, \qquad (y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 2, \: 1 \leq z \leq 3\big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/240ac546b0dd725e392dd0bd475b2ef00eebce2594be5921285e227137538c46.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=1, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(y+\sqrt{2}z)=\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(1)}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =2\cdot (2-1)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

e-12379.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the cone $z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ that is subject to the constraints  $x^2 + y^2 \leq 4,\, x\geq 0$ and $y\geq 0.$
e-12379.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \,  \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \qquad (x,y)\in D,
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x^2+y^2\leq 4, \, x\geq 0, \, y\geq 0 \big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/be8246dc3bfe1bf16af5d9913fc4e6aef58ddad282646a00d3e31120f6bf31e8.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}r\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot [\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the cylinder $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ that is bounded by the constraints $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}},\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}})^{2}+(0)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=\frac{x}{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 1 \\ u & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\text{d}u \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: For z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}, z_x=x/\sqrt{x^2+y^2} and z_y=y/\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. Thus the surface-area integrand is \sqrt{1+z_x^2+z_y^2}=\sqrt{2}. The rectangular domain has area (1-0)(2-1)=1, so the surface area is \sqrt{2}.

Question 3
?

Find the surface area of the part of the plane z=2x+3y that is bounded by the constraints 0≤x≤1 and 1≤y≤3.

a

b
43
c
214
d
14
e
314

decision.explanation: For z=2x+3y, z_x=2 and z_y=3, so the surface-area integrand is \sqrt{1+2^2+3^2}=\sqrt{14}. The rectangular domain has area (1-0)(3-1)=2, giving surface area 2\sqrt{14}.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z=2x+3y$ that is bounded by the constraints $0\le x\le 1$ and $1\le y\le 3.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2x+3y,\,0\le x\le 1,\,1\le y\le 3.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)=2, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+3y)=3,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2)^{2}+(3)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4+9}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot \text{Area}(D) \\  & =\sqrt{14}\cdot (1-0)\cdot (3-1) \\  & =2\sqrt{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

z=2x+3y,0≤x≤1,1≤y≤3.

Now, since

∂z∂x=∂∂x(2x+3y)=2,∂z∂y=∂∂y(2x+3y)=3,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(2)2+(3)2dA=∬D1+4+9dA=∬D14dA=14∬DdA=14⋅Area(D)=14⋅(1−0)⋅(3−1)=214.

The integral above gives the surface area of z=x2+2y2 for 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1. What is the missing expression?

a
1+4x2+16y2
b
1+4x2+16y2
c
1+2x2+8y2
d
1+2x2+4y2
e
1+4x2+8y2
Submit

decision.explanation: The surface-area integrand is \sqrt{1+z_x^2+z_y^2}. Since z=x^2+2y^2, its partial derivatives are z_x=2x and z_y=4y, giving \sqrt{1+4x^2+16y^2}.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of $z={x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ What is the missing expression?
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={x}^{2}+2{y}^{2},\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(4y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}.$

Question 4

∬DAAAAAAAAdA,D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1}

The integral above gives the surface area of z=x2+2y2 for 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1. What is the missing expression?

a
1+4x2+16y2
b
1+4x2+16y2
c
1+2x2+8y2
d
1+2x2+4y2
e
1+4x2+8y2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by ∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by z=x2+2y2,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1.

Now, since ∂z∂x=∂∂x(x2+2y2)=2x,∂z∂y=∂∂y(x2+2y2)=4y,

the surface area is given by ∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(2x)2+(4y)2dA=∬D1+4x2+16y2dA.

Therefore, the correct answer is 1+4x2+16y2.

decision.explanation: For z=y^2-x^3, z_x=-3x^2 and z_y=2y. The surface-area integrand is therefore \sqrt{1+z_x^2+z_y^2}=\sqrt{1+9x^4+4y^2}.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ What is the missing expression?
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={y}^{2}-{x}^{3},\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{3})=-3{x}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{3})=2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-3{x}^{2})}^{2}+{(2y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{x}^{4}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $\sqrt{1+9{x}^{4}+4{y}^{2}}.$

Question 5
?

∬DAAAAAAAAdA,D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2}

The integral above gives the surface area of z=y2−x3 for 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤2. What is the missing expression?

a
1−3x2+2y
b
1+9x4+4y2
c
1+36x4y2
d
1+36x4y2
e
1−3x2+2y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by ∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by z=y2−x3,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2.

Now, since ∂z∂x=∂∂x(y2−x3)=−3x2,∂z∂y=∂∂y(y2−x3)=2y,

the surface area is given by ∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(−3x2)2+(2y)2dA=∬D1+9x4+4y2dA.

Therefore, the correct answer is 1+9x4+4y2.

history.html:
For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by ∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by z=y2−x3,0≤x≤1,0≤y≤2.

Now, since ∂z∂x=∂∂x(y2−x3)=−3x2,∂z∂y=∂∂y(y2−x3)=2y,

the surface area is given by ∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(−3x2)2+(2y)2dA=∬D1+9x4+4y2dA.

Therefore, the correct answer is 1+9x4+4y2.

before.html:
Question 6
?

Consider the portion of the paraboloid z=x2+y2 whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by the lines y=x, x=1, and the x-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
∫01∫0x1+x+ydydx
b
∫01∫0x1+2x+2ydydx
c
∫01∫0x1+x2+y2dydx
d
∫01∫0x1+4x2+4y2dydx
e
∫01∫0x1+2x2+2y2dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: The bounded triangular domain is 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤x. Since z_x=2x and z_y=2y, the surface-area integrand is \sqrt{1+4x^2+4y^2}. Thus option d has both the correct limits and integrand.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider the portion of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by the lines $y=x,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/0b6de7829e702377d1b20bb1b297d3d28e6fb8bae9672b0137d92b4d53a96c83.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the portion of the paraboloid z=x2+y2 whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by the lines y=x, x=1, and the x-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
∫01∫0x1+x+ydydx
b
∫01∫0x1+2x+2ydydx
c
∫01∫0x1+x2+y2dydx
d
∫01∫0x1+4x2+4y2dydx
e
∫01∫0x1+2x2+2y2dydx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

z=x2+y2,(x,y)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤x},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

∂z∂x=∂∂x(x2+y2)=2x,∂z∂y=∂∂y(x2+y2)=2y,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(2x)2+(2y)2dA=∬D1+4x2+4y2dA=∫01∫0x1+4x2+4y2dydx.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms the domain 0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤x. With z_x=2x and z_y=2y, the surface-area integrand is \sqrt{1+4x^2+4y^2}, so option d is correct.

content.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains
content.problem: Consider the portion of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by the lines $y=x,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/0b6de7829e702377d1b20bb1b297d3d28e6fb8bae9672b0137d92b4d53a96c83.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the portion of the surface z=x+y3 whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by y=x2 and y=1. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
∫−11∫x212+4y2dydx
b
∫−11∫x211+ydydx
c
∫−11∫x212+3y2dydx
d
∫−11∫x212+9y4dydx
e
∫−11∫x211+3y4dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: The curves intersect at x=±1, so the domain is -1≤x≤1 and x^2≤y≤1. Since z_x=1 and z_y=3y^2, the surface-area integrand is \sqrt{1+1^2+(3y^2)^2}=\sqrt{2+9y^4}.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=x+{y}^{3}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=1.$ Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=x+{y}^{3},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 1},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/87845c65dba220978ca81bd5a2b27816ca15f951cd14d8fe499ab43d3c64ef77.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{3})=1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{3})=3{y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(1)^{2}+{(3{y}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\sqrt{2+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the portion of the surface z=x+y3 whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by y=x2 and y=1. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
∫−11∫x212+4y2dydx
b
∫−11∫x211+ydydx
c
∫−11∫x212+3y2dydx
d
∫−11∫x212+9y4dydx
e
∫−11∫x211+3y4dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

z=x+y3,(x,y)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(x,y):−1≤x≤1,x2≤y≤1},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

∂z∂x=∂∂x(x+y3)=1,∂z∂y=∂∂y(x+y3)=3y2,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(1)2+(3y2)2dA=∬D2+9y4dA=∫−11∫x212+9y4dydx.

content.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains
content.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=x+{y}^{3}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=1.$ Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=x+{y}^{3},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 1},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/87845c65dba220978ca81bd5a2b27816ca15f951cd14d8fe499ab43d3c64ef77.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{3})=1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{3})=3{y}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(1)^{2}+{(3{y}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\sqrt{2+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the portion of the surface z=xy2 whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by y=x2, x=1, and the x-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
 ∫01∫0x21+y+xydydx
b
 ∫01∫0x21+2y4+2x2y2dydx
c
 ∫01∫0x21+y2+2xydydx
d
 ∫01∫0x21+y4+4x2y2dydx
e
 ∫01∫0x21+y2+2x2ydydx
Submit

decision.explanation: The bounded domain is 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤x^2. For z=xy^2, z_x=y^2 and z_y=2xy, so the surface-area integrand is \sqrt{1+y^4+4x^2y^2}. This gives option d.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=x{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y={x}^{2},$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=x{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/1419b067fe92945249655c5d29498aa4d3b0269d79ebd237fd9ed2a713b70b6a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})={y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})=2xy,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({y}^{2})}^{2}+(2xy)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the portion of the surface z=xy2 whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by y=x2, x=1, and the x-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.

a
 ∫01∫0x21+y+xydydx
b
 ∫01∫0x21+2y4+2x2y2dydx
c
 ∫01∫0x21+y2+2xydydx
d
 ∫01∫0x21+y4+4x2y2dydx
e
 ∫01∫0x21+y2+2x2ydydx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

z=xy2,(x,y)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(x,y):0≤x≤1,0≤y≤x2},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

∂z∂x=∂∂x(xy2)=y2,∂z∂y=∂∂y(xy2)=2xy,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(y2)2+(2xy)2dA=∬D1+y4+4x2y2dA=∫01∫0x21+y4+4x2y2dydx.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms z_x=y^2 and z_y=2xy, giving the integrand \sqrt{1+y^4+4x^2y^2}. The bounded domain is 0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤x^2, so option d is correct.

content.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains
content.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=x{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y={x}^{2},$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=x{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/1419b067fe92945249655c5d29498aa4d3b0269d79ebd237fd9ed2a713b70b6a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})={y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})=2xy,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({y}^{2})}^{2}+(2xy)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since z_x=x and z_y=0, the area is ∫ from -1 to 1 ∫ from 0 to 1/√(1+x²) of √(1+x²) dy dx. Integrating over y cancels the square-root factor, leaving ∫ from -1 to 1 of 1 dx=2.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/b9504140a4827cd74b74e8c23f76e1305389f1bc93a87834a37d4b20222e56f0.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})=x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(x)^{2}+(0)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1/\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{1/\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =1-(-1) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

z=x22,(x,y)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(x,y):−1≤x≤1,0≤y≤11+x2},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

∂z∂x=∂∂x(x22)=x,∂z∂y=∂∂y(x22)=0,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(x)2+(0)2dA=∬D1+x2dA=∫−11∫01/1+x21+x2dydx=∫−111+x2⋅y|01/1+x2dx=∫−111+x2⋅11+x2dx=∫−11dx=x|−11=1−(−1)=2.

before.html:
Question 10
?

Find the surface area of the portion of the surface z=3sin⁡x+22y whose projection onto the xy-plane is bounded by y=sin⁡2x and the x-axis from x=0 to x=π2.

a
 22−3
b
 42−2
c
 6−2
d
 82
e
 4
Submit

decision.explanation: Here z_x=3\cos(x) and z_y=2\sqrt{2}, so the area is 3\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1+\cos^2(x)}\sin(2x)\,dx. Substituting u=1+\cos^2(x), du=-\sin(2x)dx, gives 3\int_1^2\sqrt{u}\,du=2(2^{3/2}-1)=4\sqrt{2}-2.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡2x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/f6200343142274ee2f5b3934cbe014ee24edf8177f3a544c38dc070bb7df83ef.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=2\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{cos}^{2}⁡x+8}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{9(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{cos}^{2}⁡x,$ we get $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{\pi }{2} \\ u & 2 & 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{2}^{1}\sqrt{u}(-\text{d}u) \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2({2}^{3/2}-1) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{sin}⁡2x},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/f6200343142274ee2f5b3934cbe014ee24edf8177f3a544c38dc070bb7df83ef.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡x+2\sqrt{2}y)=2\sqrt{2},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{cos}^{2}⁡x+8}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{9(1+{cos}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{cos}^{2}⁡x,$ we get $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{\pi }{2} \\ u & 2 & 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{2}^{1}\sqrt{u}(-\text{d}u) \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2({2}^{3/2}-1) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 11
?

∬DAAAAAdA,D={(x,z):AAAAAA}

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface y=1xz that lies inside the cylinder x2+z2=2. From left to right, what are the missing expressions?

a
1+x+zx4z4 and x2+z2=2
b
x2+z2xz and x2+z2≤2
c
1xz and x2+z2=2
d
1+x2+z2x4z4 and x2+z2≤2
e
1+x+zx2z2 and x2+z2≥2
Submit

decision.explanation: For y=1/(xz), y_x=-1/(x^2z) and y_z=-1/(xz^2). Thus the area integrand is sqrt(1+(x^2+z^2)/(x^4z^4)). Inside the cylinder means x^2+z^2≤2, giving option d. The axes xz=0 are excluded implicitly because the surface is undefined there; the integral is improper and diverges.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(x,z)\,:\,\boxed{}\,}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\frac{1}{xz}$ that lies inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\frac{1}{xz},\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}{z}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{z}^{4}}}\,$ and ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.$

Question 11
?

∬DAAAAAdA,D={(x,z):AAAAAA}

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface y=1xz that lies inside the cylinder x2+z2=2. From left to right, what are the missing expressions?

a
1+x+zx4z4 and x2+z2=2
b
x2+z2xz and x2+z2≤2
c
1xz and x2+z2=2
d
1+x2+z2x4z4 and x2+z2≤2
e
1+x+zx2z2 and x2+z2≥2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by y=f(x,z) with (x,z)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂y∂x)2+(∂y∂z)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

y=1xz,x2+z2≤2.

Now, since

∂y∂x=∂∂x(1xz)=−1x2z,∂y∂z=∂∂z(1xz)=−1xz2,

the surface area is

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂y∂x)2+(∂y∂z)2dA=∬D1+(−1x2z)2+(−1xz2)2dA=∬D1+1x4z2+1x2z4dA=∬D1+x2+z2x4z4dA.

Therefore, the correct answer is

1+x2+z2x4z4 and x2+z2≤2.

content.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as X=F(Y,Z) or Y=F(X,Z)
content.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(x,z)\,:\,\boxed{}\,}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\frac{1}{xz}$ that lies inside the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\frac{1}{xz},\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{1}{xz})=-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}z})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{x{z}^{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{x}^{4}{z}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{z}^{4}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}{{x}^{4}{z}^{4}}}\,$ and ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.$

Question 12
?

Find the surface area of the part of the surface x=ey−z whose projection onto the yz-plane is bounded by z=e2y, y=0, y=12, and the y-axis.

a
e+2−3
b
2(e−1)3/23
c
3(e+2)3/2+934
d
2−33+e
e
(e+2)3/2−333
Submit

decision.explanation: For x=e^y-z, x_y=e^y and x_z=-1, giving the area factor \sqrt{2+e^{2y}}. The domain is 0≤y≤1/2 and 0≤z≤e^{2y}, so A=\int_0^{1/2}e^{2y}\sqrt{2+e^{2y}}\,dy. With u=2+e^{2y}, this becomes (1/2)\int_3^{e+2}\sqrt{u}\,du=((e+2)^{3/2}-3\sqrt{3})/3.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $x={e}^{y}-z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by $z={e}^{2y},$ $y=0,$ $y=\frac{1}{2},$ and the $y$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={e}^{y}-z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le z\le {e}^{2y}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/9cae5b68f77c2d79df8a81d0421146ac2bbe618c6065a457c33c86caceeb1327.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}-z)={e}^{y}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y}-z)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({e}^{y})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{2y}}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z={e}^{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u={e}^{2y}+2,$ we get $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1/2 \\ u & 3 & e+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{3}^{e+2}\frac{1}{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{e+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((e+2)^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{(e+2)^{3/2}-3\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by x=f(y,z) with (y,z)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂x∂z)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

x=ey−z,(y,z)∈D,

where

D={(y,z):0≤y≤12,0≤z≤e2y},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

∂x∂y=∂∂y(ey−z)=ey,∂x∂z=∂∂z(ey−z)=−1,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂x∂z)2dA=∬D1+(ey)2+(−1)2dA=∬De2y+2dA=∫01/2∫0e2ye2y+2dzdy=∫01/2e2y+2⋅z|z=0z=e2ydy=∫01/2e2y+2⋅e2ydy.

Setting u=e2y+2, we get du=2e2ydy. Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

y01/2u3e+2

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

∫01/2e2y+2⋅e2ydy=∫3e+212u1/2du=13u3/2|3e+2=13((e+2)3/2−33/2)=(e+2)3/2−333.

content.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as X=F(Y,Z) or Y=F(X,Z)
content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $x={e}^{y}-z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by $z={e}^{2y},$ $y=0,$ $y=\frac{1}{2},$ and the $y$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={e}^{y}-z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{1}{2},\,0\le z\le {e}^{2y}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/9cae5b68f77c2d79df8a81d0421146ac2bbe618c6065a457c33c86caceeb1327.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y}-z)={e}^{y}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{y}-z)=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+({e}^{y})^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{2y}}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z={e}^{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u={e}^{2y}+2,$ we get $\text{d}u=2{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1/2 \\ u & 3 & e+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\sqrt{{e}^{2y}+2}\cdot {e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{3}^{e+2}\frac{1}{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{3}^{e+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((e+2)^{3/2}-{3}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{(e+2)^{3/2}-3\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The projection is 0≤y≤1, 0≤z≤y. Since x_y=2y and x_z=\sqrt{3}, the area factor is \sqrt{1+4y^2+3}=2\sqrt{1+y^2}. Thus A=\int_0^1 2y\sqrt{1+y^2}\,dy=\frac{2}{3}[(1+y^2)^{3/2}]_0^1=\frac{2}{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $x={y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by $z=y,$ $y=1,$ and the $y$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le y},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/0cf571155f2a4cd78d83c4808326cd8102badb3c22f43e00d95aee2494859f48.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z)=2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z)=\sqrt{3},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{4+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{y}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=2y\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 2\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by x=f(y,z) with (y,z)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂x∂z)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

x=y2+3z,(y,z)∈D,

where

D={(y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤y},

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

∂x∂y=∂∂y(y2+3z)=2y,∂x∂z=∂∂z(y2+3z)=3,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂x∂z)2dA=∬D1+(2y)2+(3)2dA=∬D4+4y2dA=∬D21+y2dA=2∫01∫0y1+y2dzdy=2∫011+y2⋅z|z=0z=ydy=2∫011+y2⋅ydy.

Setting u=1+y2, we get du=2ydy. Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

y01u12

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

2∫011+y2⋅ydy=∫12u1/2du=23u3/2|12=23(23/2−13/2)=23(22−1).

content.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as X=F(Y,Z) or Y=F(X,Z)
content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $x={y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z$ whose projection onto the $yz$-plane is bounded by $z=y,$ $y=1,$ and the $y$-axis.
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z,\,(y,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le z\le y},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/0cf571155f2a4cd78d83c4808326cd8102badb3c22f43e00d95aee2494859f48.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z)=2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+\sqrt{3}z)=\sqrt{3},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{4+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+{y}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=2y\,\text{d}y.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & 0 & 1 \\ u & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+{y}^{2}}\cdot y\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({2}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

Find the surface area of the part of the surface y=sin⁡x+z whose projection onto the xz-plane is bounded by z=sin⁡(2x) and the x-axis for 0≤x≤π2.

a
23(33−1)
b
12(22−1)
c
23(ππ−1)
d
23(33−22)
e
32
Submit

decision.explanation: Since y_x=\cos(x) and y_z=1, the area is A=\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(2x)\sqrt{2+\cos^2(x)}\,dx. Set u=2+\cos^2(x), so du=-\sin(2x)dx. Then A=\int_2^3\sqrt{u}\,du=\frac{2}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{2}).

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+z$ whose projection onto the $xz$-plane is bounded by $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ and the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+z,\,(x,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le z\le \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/be5dc3bf3ed4b6b7bee06d583b69e40a3922edede1e61a6f0b68d2ce0767f92a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+z)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=2+{cos}^{2}⁡x,$ we get $\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{\pi }{2} \\ u & 3 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{3}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({3}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+z,\,(x,z)\in D,
$$

where 

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le z\le \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/be5dc3bf3ed4b6b7bee06d583b69e40a3922edede1e61a6f0b68d2ce0767f92a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+z)=1,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{2}+(1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot z\,{|}_{z=0}^{z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=2+{cos}^{2}⁡x,$ we get $\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{\pi }{2} \\ u & 3 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\sqrt{2+{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{3}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}\,{|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({3}^{3/2}-{2}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}(3\sqrt{3}-2\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

∬DAAAAAAAAdA,D={(y,z):AAAAAA}

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface x=y3+ez that lies inside the elliptical cylinder y24+z29=1. From left to right, what are the missing expressions?

a
2y4+ez and y24+z29=1
b
y3+e2z−1 and y24+z29≥1
c
1+9y4+e2z and y24+z29≤1
d
1+9y2+e2z and y24+z29≥1
e
2y2+ez and y24+z29≤1
Submit

decision.explanation: For x=y^3+e^z, x_y=3y^2 and x_z=e^z. The surface-area integrand is therefore √(1+9y^4+e^{2z}). Inside the elliptical cylinder corresponds to y^2/4+z^2/9≤1, so both expressions match option c.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(y,z)\,:\,\boxed{}\,}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z}$ that lies inside the elliptical cylinder $\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}=1.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z},\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})=3{y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})={e}^{z},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2})}^{2}+({e}^{z})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,$ and $\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.$

Question 15
?

∬DAAAAAAAAdA,D={(y,z):AAAAAA}

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface x=y3+ez that lies inside the elliptical cylinder y24+z29=1. From left to right, what are the missing expressions?

a
2y4+ez and y24+z29=1
b
y3+e2z−1 and y24+z29≥1
c
1+9y4+e2z and y24+z29≤1
d
1+9y2+e2z and y24+z29≥1
e
2y2+ez and y24+z29≤1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by x=f(y,z) with (y,z)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂x∂z)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

x=y3+ez,y24+z29≤1.

Now, since

∂x∂y=∂∂y(y3+ez)=3y2,∂x∂z=∂∂z(y3+ez)=ez,

the surface area is

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂y∂z)2dA=∬D1+(3y2)2+(ez)2dA=∬D1+9y4+e2zdA.

Therefore, the correct answer is

1+9y4+e2z and y24+z29≤1.

content.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(y,z)\,:\,\boxed{}\,}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z}$ that lies inside the elliptical cylinder $\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}=1.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x={y}^{3}+{e}^{z},\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.
$$

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})=3{y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{3}+{e}^{z})={e}^{z},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2})}^{2}+({e}^{z})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\,$ $\sqrt{1+9{y}^{4}+{e}^{2z}}\,$ and $\,\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{9}\le 1.$

decision.explanation: For z=2y-x, z_x=-1 and z_y=2, so the surface-area factor is √(1+1+4)=√6. The domain is a semicircle of radius 3, with area 9π/2. Thus the surface area is 9π√6/2.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z=2y-x$ that is subject to the constraints ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9$ and $x\le 0.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2y-x,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9,\,x\le 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/3c6c556ec90138fa1f0b599c6afed9d093e5c1b10f7751a5fbe55f0add617e1d.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-1)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+1+4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$

Question 16

Find the surface area of the part of the plane z=2y−x that is subject to the constraints x2+y2≤9 and x≤0.

a
 9π2
b
9π62
c
 9π(6−1)4
d
 3π22
e
 2π63
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=f(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

z=2y−x,(x,y)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(x,y):x2+y2≤9,x≤0},

as shown below.

Now, since

∂z∂x=∂∂x(2y−x)=−1,∂z∂y=∂∂y(2y−x)=2,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D1+(−1)2+(2)2dA=∬D1+1+4dA=∬D6dA.

In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region D can be expressed as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,π2≤θ≤3π2}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain ∬D6dA=∬Δ6rdrdθ=∫π/23π/2∫036rdrdθ=6∫π/23π/2dθ∫03rdr=6⋅[θ]π/23π/2⋅[r22]03=6⋅π⋅92=9π62.

content.knowledge_point: Changing to Polar Coordinates
content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the plane $z=2y-x$ that is subject to the constraints ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9$ and $x\le 0.$
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=2y-x,\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9,\,x\le 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/3c6c556ec90138fa1f0b599c6afed9d093e5c1b10f7751a5fbe55f0add617e1d.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y-x)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-1)^{2}+(2)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+1+4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{6}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{6}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot [\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi \sqrt{6}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since z_x=-2x and z_y=-2y, the area factor is √(1+4x²+4y²). In polar coordinates, A=2π∫₀³r√(1+4r²)dr=π/6[(1+4r²)^{3/2}]₀³=π(37√37−1)/6.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/d2774aa4a85d25c4e35f3eb327adc82f9ef02eceb2be31ddf730493797e4cac2.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2x)^{2}+(-2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 3 \\ u & 1 & 37\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{37}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(37)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (37\sqrt{37}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9.$
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/d2774aa4a85d25c4e35f3eb327adc82f9ef02eceb2be31ddf730493797e4cac2.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2x)^{2}+(-2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 3 \\ u & 1 & 37\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{37}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{37}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{37} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(37)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (37\sqrt{37}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by y=f(x,z) with (x,z)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂y∂x)2+(∂y∂z)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

y=1−x2+z2,(x,z)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(x,z):x2+z2≤2},

as shown below.

Now, since

∂y∂x=∂∂x(1−x2+z2)=−2x,∂y∂z=∂∂z(1−x2+z2)=2z,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂y∂x)2+(∂y∂z)2dA=∬D1+(−2x)2+(2z)2dA=∬D1+4x2+4z2dA=∬D1+4(x2+z2)dA.

In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region D can be expressed as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤2,0≤θ≤2π}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain ∬D1+4(x2+z2)dA=∬Δ1+4r2rdrdθ=∫02π∫02r1+4r2drdθ=∫02πdθ∫02r1+4r2dr=2π∫02r1+4r2dr.

Setting u=1+4r2, we get du=8rdr. Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

r02u19

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

2π∫02r1+4r2dr=2π⋅18∫19udu=π4∫19u1/2du=π4⋅23[u3/2]19=π6[u3/2]19=π6(27−1)=13π3.

content.knowledge_point: Changing to Polar Coordinates
content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the hyperbolic paraboloid $y=1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2.$
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $y=f(x,z)$ with $(x,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
y=1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2},\,(x,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 2},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/ab855ef2b9b5363005c14ea37470ed9ecb5853380a301341d20e2cd6095a5d1f.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂y}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2})=-2x, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(1-{x}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂y}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂y}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(-2x)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({x}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ u & 1 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The surface-area factor is √(1+z_x²+z_y²)=2/√(4−x²−y²). The domain is a half disk, so in polar coordinates A=∫₀^π∫₀¹2r/√(4−r²) dr dθ=2π(2−√3).

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ that is subject to the constraints ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1$ and $y\ge 0.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1,\,y\ge 0},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/e7cb4d16f39d1c1e38d65000471cbc5ca1831a0bbc2cfc61c4f03d087d6a5125.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=4-{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=-2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 4 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r & =-\pi {\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{4}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi \cdot 2{({u}^{1/2})}_{3}^{4} \\  & =2\pi \cdot ({4}^{1/2}-{3}^{1/2}) \\  & =2\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}+{(-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{\frac{4}{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=4-{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=-2r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & 1 \\ u & 4 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2r}{\sqrt{4-{r}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r & =-\pi {\int }_{4}^{3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi {\int }_{3}^{4}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\pi \cdot 2{({u}^{1/2})}_{3}^{4} \\  & =2\pi \cdot ({4}^{1/2}-{3}^{1/2}) \\  & =2\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the paraboloid $x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3.$
after.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/66b05919a7644818eea7265ff3ae8fc3ced4ac7d1d6d30352f612649393c876a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & \sqrt{3} \\ u & 1 & 13\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{13}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{13}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(13)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (13\sqrt{13}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}

For a surface S defined by x=f(y,z) with (y,z)∈D, the surface area of S is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂x∂z)2dA.

In this case, our surface is given by

x=5+y2+z2,(y,z)∈D

where the region D is given by

D={(y,z):y2+z2≤3},

as shown below.

Now, since

∂x∂y=∂∂y(5+y2+z2)=2y,∂x∂z=∂∂z(5+y2+z2)=2z,

the surface area is given by

∬SdS=∬D1+(∂x∂y)2+(∂x∂z)2dA=∬D1+(2y)2+(2z)2dA=∬D1+4y2+4z2dA=∬D1+4(y2+z2)dA.

In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region D can be expressed as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,0≤θ≤2π}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain ∬D1+4(y2+z2)dA=∬Δ1+4r2rdrdθ=∫02π∫03r1+4r2drdθ=∫02πdθ∫03r1+4r2dr=2π∫03r1+4r2dr.

Setting u=1+4r2, we get du=8rdr. Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

content.knowledge_point: Changing to Polar Coordinates
content.problem: Find the surface area of the part of the paraboloid $x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ that is subject to the constraint ${y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3.$
content.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
x=5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},\,(y,z)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}\le 3},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/66b05919a7644818eea7265ff3ae8fc3ced4ac7d1d6d30352f612649393c876a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2y, \\ \frac{∂x}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(5+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂x}{∂y})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂x}{∂z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}+(2z)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+4({y}^{2}+{z}^{2})}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $u=1+4{r}^{2},$ we get $\text{d}u=8r\,\text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & 0 & \sqrt{3} \\ u & 1 & 13\end{aligned}
$$

 

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}r\sqrt{1+4{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{13}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{13}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{13} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(13)^{3/2}-1] \\  & =\frac{\pi (13\sqrt{13}-1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
